title: The server code every route loads
headline: One import cycle of 229 files in src/server makes 181 of 268 route handlers, 559 of 562 pages and the proxy each load about 10 MB of server code (the AI manager's tools, the admin's whole text in two languages, the schema, Stripe, sharp): a fat route takes 0.9 to 1.3 s and 97 MB of heap to load cold on this machine against 0.16 to 0.24 s and 26 MB for /api/health, and every instance first pays 0.27 to 0.30 s for a start hook and about 0.09 s to read a 10.4 MB list of server references. None of it depends on what a store uses, so it grows with stores, traffic and the deploy on every push once the platform opens. The cure is a few dozen small import changes, not removed features: one import path takes the visit beacon from 10.4 to 1.9 MB (0.96 MB with the schema and Stripe cuts), the rest take a storefront page from 11.3 to about 3.5 MB, the proxy from 9.2 to 2.4 MB (0.8 MB with its readers split) and 2.2 MB off 384 admin pages (all simulated on the build's own module graph). A scan test and a byte budget must land with them or the next convenient import undoes the work; before opening is the cheapest time, with no live traffic and every cut checkable on the next build.

clean: A lean route is possible today: /api/health loads 16 chunks and 1.1 MB, and 24 handlers reach under 500 modules (/admin/sw.js 93, /api/ucp/catalogue.json 103, /api/gravatar/[hash] 139). The fat graph is a tangle of imports, not a property of the stack.

Turbopack runs a module's body only when it is first imported: a chunk's factories are registered on load and the route's own code is loaded on the first request. /api/visit's chunks hold 1,879 source modules; 1,332 factories run.

A lazy server import is safe in a prerendered page: the server runtime loads an async chunk with a synchronous require and returns an already resolved promise (.next/server/chunks/[turbopack]_runtime.js:945-970), so import() adds no I/O task. What it does not do is shrink the function's package: code behind import() is still traced.

Modules are instantiated once per process, so a second fat route in a warm instance costs almost nothing when it names the same chunk files (/api/shop/tiles after /api/visit: 1 ms). The exception is SG-11's copies.
Heavy third-party parsers are already behind import(): unpdf, mammoth, playwright-core, @sparticuz/chromium (58 await import() in 30 server files). They cost package size, not cold-start time.

sameSite() already lives in a leaf with no imports (src/lib/same-site.ts), OwnerToolError in its own leaf (src/server/owner-tool-error.ts), visitorKey in chat-turns.ts, and 66 src/lib modules already import their own area's admin catalogue directly: several of the moves are only import-path changes with a pattern in the repo.
The taxonomy (12.7 MiB of JSON) is read from disk on first use and kept per instance (src/server/product-taxonomy.ts:27-43); catalog.ts reads it only for a product with a standard category.
Chromium, the PDF files, the docs' Markdown and HarfBuzz are traced only into the routes that use them (next.config.ts:50-78); only the taxonomy uses '/**'.
The database pool is made on first use (src/db/client.ts:94-97); importing the client opens nothing.
Source maps are not traced into any function checked, and the edge runtime carries nothing heavy (.next/server/edge is 116 KB).
The browser's copy of the admin catalogue is already split per area (D540, docs/performance.md:167-185); what is whole is the server's registry (SG-4).

After the planned cuts no second hub hides behind the first on an admin page: removing any one file of src/server or src/app from /admin/[store]/orders takes off at most 238 modules and 0.64 MB. An admin page's floor of about 2,000 modules is what it uses (auth, orders, checkout), plus the text registry.
The three-minute type check is not paid on Vercel (next.config.ts:45, D378) and CI runs it in its own job: it is no cost of the server graph.

Test coupling to the present import paths is small for the P0 and P1 cuts: one mock of the chat module, one proxy test with five mocks, nothing for the cycle's edges, the key reader or the theme store section. Only SG-9 meets many tests (113 files).

No finding in this dimension asks to retire, hide or merge a feature, and none argues from a feature being unused. Each is a running cost that every store pays whatever it uses, so the owner's clarification changes wording (SG-5), not substance.

findings.evidence: sameSite() lives in src/lib/same-site.ts and imports nothing. chat-route.ts re-exports it (line 38) and also imports chat-agent.ts, private-mode.ts, shop.ts and support.ts (lines 7-12). I counted the importers again: 61 non-test files import chat-route; 37 take only sameSite and 16 take fail and sameSite (53 route files), replicate-route.ts and assistant-route.ts take sameSite, and only the two chat routes and four support modules use anything else. findings.title: One import cycle of 229 server files makes almost every route load everything
findings.evidence: 229 files of src/server form one import cycle (712 edges; Tarjan on the build's own module graph, reproduced by the skeptic and matched by the tests-ci plan's source-level count). The build compiles it once per layer (route handlers, pages, proxy). It reaches 1,934 modules and 10.3 MB. 181 of 268 handlers and 559 of 562 pages reach it. I traced the entry chains again on the graph: a storefront page enters through pages.ts -> visibility.ts -> customers.ts; /api/shop/tiles through chat-route.ts -> chat-agent.ts -> recommend.ts -> customers.ts; /api/cron/page-jobs through site-tools.ts -> pages.ts -> visibility.ts -> customers.ts; from customers.ts all go privacy-erasure.ts -> retention.ts -> order-rules.ts -> follow-ups.ts -> owner-tools.ts. The upward edges are small. customers.ts:17 imports the GDPR erasure job for one call in deleteCustomer (line 500). visibility.ts:17 takes one SQL fragment, bought, from customer-admin.ts:25. store-features.ts:35 calls storeObligations once (line 52), a plain count that lives in store-closure.ts:87-110 beside the code that closes a store. follow-ups.ts:14 and manager-tools.ts:50 import OwnerToolError from owner-tools.ts although it is defined in the leaf owner-tool-error.ts. I re-ran the simulation: on the storefront home page three cuts do all the work (2,498 -> 2,044 -> 2,040 -> 1,843 module paths; 11.3 -> 7.7 MB); the other proposed cuts change nothing there but shrink other routes (seo.ts -> theme-store.ts takes 90 modules and sharp off /api/shop/tiles). With every cut of this plan in the graph (this finding, SG-3, SG-4 step a, SG-6, SG-15, SG-17, SG-18) the median handler goes from 2,015 to 725 module paths, the median storefront page from 2,500 to 1,637, handlers over 1,500 from 181 to 29 (the 29 are the AI manager's and the MCP's routes, support's, two personal-data export routes, the Admin API and four cron routes, which use what they load).
findings.cost: 0.9 to 1.3 s and 97 MB of heap (222 MB RSS) to load a fat route cold on this machine, against 0.16 to 0.24 s and 26 MB for /api/health (the skeptic's re-measurement, fresh process per run). About 0.3 s of it is running module bodies; the rest is compiling, which a bytecode cache on the host would shorten (not checked). 10 to 12 MB of server chunks per route.

findings.title: Every cold function reads a 10.4 MB list of server references before its first request
findings.evidence: Next's route module loads server/server-reference-manifest.json for every app route, pages and route handlers alike, in prepare() before the first request (route-module.js:206-212 and 463-465; the app-route template calls it at line 132). loadManifest reads the file, parses it and deep-freezes it, once per process (load-manifest.external.js:40-66). The file is 10,397,955 bytes. Timed with Next's own loadManifest in a fresh node process, 3 runs: 80 to 91 ms and 20 to 24 MB of heap (39 MB of RSS); split: read 20 ms, parse 40 to 43 ms, deep freeze 30 ms. The other manifests a route loads add about 26 ms and 7 MB (prerender-manifest.json 2.0 MB: 13.6 ms; routes-manifest.json 0.5 MB: 6 ms). None of this is in the cold-load figures above, which time only the route's chunks. Why it is so large: it lists 1,454 references, each with one entry per route whose bundle holds it: 81,027 entries. 85 of the references are 'use cache' functions and they hold 55,974 of the entries: 74 of the 85 are listed for more than 700 of the 807 routes, because the cycle of SG-1 puts every cached reader in every route (the widest, a cached read in stores.ts, is listed for 804). The 1,369 server actions hold 25,053 entries (30 of them are listed for 420 routes: the admin shell's account actions). A model of the manifest from the build's graph (for each route, the references whose file it reaches by sync imports) gives 78,743 entries today against the real 81,027, and 67,681 with the cuts of SG-1, SG-3, SG-4 step a, SG-6 and SG-15 in.
findings.cost: 80 to 91 ms and 20 to 24 MB of heap per cold instance of every function, the lean ones included: about a third on top of /api/health's 0.16 to 0.24 s. Measured here with Next's own loader; whether Vercel's packaging changes how the file is read was not checked.
findings.who_pays: The server per cold instance of every function, whatever the route. It grows with routes times references: each new cached reader adds about 660 entries today, each new route about 100.
fix_steps: Measure it where it matters first: Next traces this step as the span 'load route manifests' (route-module.js:463-465). Read that span for one cold request in production (or log the time around the first request once) to confirm the function pays what this machine shows.

Put the file's size and its entry count in the report of scripts/route-budget.mjs (SG-14) with a budget of today's 10.4 MB and 81,027 entries that may only fall, so growth is seen at the push that causes it.

Land SG-1, SG-3, SG-15 and SG-17: a route that no longer bundles every cached reader is no longer listed for it. Expect about 14% fewer entries (the model: 78,743 -> 67,681) and read the real number from the next build.

findings.title: getStore() imports the Stripe SDK to learn which payment modes have keys
findings.evidence: stores.ts:182 imports platformModes from stripe.ts to decide paymentsOn (line 300); orders.ts:23 does the same (line 555); stripe.ts imports the Stripe package at the top (line 3). The SDK is 189 modules and 212 KB in the server chunks. platformModes() is not a pure read of the environment today: it calls platformStripe(mode), which builds a Stripe client when a key is set (stripe.ts:33-46); its answer depends only on whether the two keys have the right shape (platformKey in src/lib/stripe-account.ts:17-26). 16 non-test files import platformModes. The price of moving it is in the tests: 113 test files mention platformModes, nearly all in a vi.mock of ./stripe that answers ['test'] (rg, counted here; the skeptic counted 98 integration files).
findings.cost: 212 KB and about 190 modules per cold start of every route that reads a store and has no other path to Stripe (6 ms measured for Stripe's own factory; the rest is parsing).
fix_steps: Not now. Do SG-18 first: it removes the commoner path to the SDK (ai.ts and mollie.ts -> settings.ts -> connect.ts) with no test to change.

Keep the 113 test files unchanged with one shared setup file (the unit config already has src/test/eager-lazy-views.ts as the pattern for a vi.mock in a setup file; add the new file to setupFiles in vitest.config.mts and vitest.integration.config.mts): vi.mock('@/server/stripe-modes', async () => { const stripe = await import('@/server/stripe'); return { platformModes: () => stripe.platformModes() }; }); Each test file's own mock of ./stripe then still decides the modes, as today, and a file with no mock gets the real answer from the environment.

findings.title: Four storefront languages are imported for every server route; a request needs one
findings.evidence: i18n.ts statically imports da, en, nb and sv (about 95 KB of source each, plus their returns, quotes, reviews and exchange parts): 413 KB in 26 modules on /api/visit.
